In algorithms and complexity we focus on the asymptotic complexity of algorithms, i.e. the amount of resources an algorithm uses as the size of the input goes to infinity.

In practice, what is needed is an algorithm that would work fast on a finite (although possibly very large) number of instances.

An algorithm which works well in practice on the finite number of instances that we are interested in doesn't need to have good asymptotic complexity (good performance on a finite number of instances doesn't imply anything regarding the asymptotic complexity). Similarly, an algorithm with good asymptotic complexity may not work well in practice on the finite number of instances that we are interested in (e.g. because of large constants).

Why do we use asymptotic complexity? How do these asymptotic analysis related to design of algorithms in practice?
answer: As noted in Raphael's answer, exact computation of worst-case running time can be very difficult. Exact computation can also be unnecessary since the RAM model already introduces approximations. For example, do all operations really take equal time? Specific implementations (hardware, optimizations) might speed up an algorithm by constant factors. We want to understand how effective an algorithm is independent of these factors. This is a big motivation for the use of asymptotic analysis.

answer:
If an index is very small (I believe less than 8 pages) it will use mixed extents. Therefore, it'll appear as if there is still fragmentation remaining, as the housing extent will contain pages from multiple indexes.

Use a Left Join instead of an Inner Join.

there is huge memory for the entire db to live in memory,

the table being queried has no indexing,

**4) Don't ring a dinner bell if you can't serve a meal** Simply put, guns are loud, like a dinner bell. Don't shoot a gun if you don't have enough lead for everybody. If you must eliminate a zombie, use a long range melee weapon like an ax or a silent ranged weapon like a crossbow.

**6) Whack it, don't double tap it** If the zombie is down, but not out, use a melee weapon, and save a bullet.
**7) Beware of disease** Just because the zombies are around doesn't mean Eboli has gone, in fact their putrid bodies can spread diseases. Always properly cook your meals and boil your water.
**8) Keep your environment in mind** Learn the exits, the walls, the dead-ends, the dangerous and safe areas. Don't stumble into a horde of zombies by mistake.
**9) Follow the four rules of gun safety** Simply put, don't shoot your buddies by being an idiot.
**10) Use your brain and break the rules** If you need to get rid of a bandit camp in a walmart, break in and burn the place down. question: " I don't have a heart. " She tapped her chest and a hatch opened, exposing whirring gears and a compartment. " But if I did, it would belong to you. " Reaching in, she pulled something out.
answer:
Three years.
It had been three years since I last saw her. Since I watched her braid her oak-colored hair. Since I felt her fingers, intertwining with mine as if our hands had been made for one another. Her grasp had been so warm.
" I've missed you." She said. She blinked in that way only she could - slowly, pensively. Like a closing flower, filled with iridescent blue.
" I've missed you, too..." It was all I could say. She pulled me closer, pressed her lips to mine. I felt her hand brush up against my own.
Her fingers were so cold.
I pushed her away, trying to ignore the hurt on her face. " No. No I can't."
" Why not?" She asked. She stepped forward, embracing me with arms like polished marble. Flawless. Just as I remembered.
Almost.
" Memories. It's just... I just can't." I pushed her away again.
" Am I not beautiful enough?" She asked, and I felt another pang of pain impale my heart like an icicle.
" No, it's not that. You're perfect. Almost... too perfect."
" Then why?" She asked. " You wanted this... I'm only here again because of you."
Before I could stop her, she grasped my palm and placed it on her chest. It vibrated softly, almost as if blood truly pumped through her veins. " Feel the life you gave me..." She said, a smile playing on her familiar lips. " it is a gift. The *ultimate* gift... and I would do anything to repay you for your kindness."
A patch of skin receded at my touch, exposing a nest of whirring gears. " I may not have a heart... but if I did, it would belong to you."
" W... where did you get *that*?" I asked, pointing into the metallic cavity. A silver locket, suspended on a chain, hung precariously within her metal frame.
With an inhumanly quick step, she withdrew from my touch. " Please, don't be angry... I found it on your bedside. I... I thought you might..."
" That belonged to *Angela*." I growled.
" But I am-"
" No. You aren't." I said flatly. " Computer, terminate program."
" No! Please!" She grabbed at my sleeves, pulling them to her chest. " Please, I'll do anything! Anything! I can *be* her, just give me a chance to learn!" Tears shone in her eyes.
" Computer... freeze subject 865. Begin dismantling procedures and diagnostics." I turned away.
" Please..." The woman who was not Angela whispered. She went to move after me, moving as if she were underwater. And then she was still - a beautiful statue... and nothing more.
I swallowed hard.
" Next time... next time she will come back to me."
" She has to."

Not so much to the reader, but to an audience. The scene is a man with powers, mutations, whatever, speaking for his fellow mutants to a religion through a local church
Eden crouched calmly and gently retrieved the crucifix from the stage, brushing the dust from its' face with his thumb. The long silver chain swung gently as he turned, once more, to the crowd. He stared deeply at the trinket in his left hand and spoke quietly.
" You think me less than human: a vile, uncivilized creature. You call me a demon and all manner of despicable things. You shout your curses at me. You demand your government imprison me not for what I have done, but what I can do... What I might do. " You demand justice for imagined slights. You assume my existence is all the proof you need for my punishment and declare a war of faith against me." His gaze slowly rose to me the crowd. His eyes glowing an unearthly, vibrant blue. His voice grew louder and more direct.
" You attack me in broad daylight. You drag me into the streets. You beat me. You push and you push and have the audacity to claim I haven't the right to push back and have the nerve to cry victim when I do. You labor, endlessly, under the apocalyptic misapprehension that you hold the mantle of your god's chosen warriors and act as generals to the Throne, but you do not!" In his rage, he smacked the pulpit from the stage and sent it sailing across the church where it exploded against the eastern wall.
The loud metal thunk of his boots hitting the floor echoed as he stepped from the stage. His breath was heavy and fast as his right arm gripped the hilt of his sword. " Pray... All of you. Pray for a hero, pray for salvation, pray for me, I care not; but get on your knees and pray." He clenched his left hand causing the crucifix to shatter and rain shrapnel to the floor.

question: " Loyalty to The State. Commitment to The Program. Service to The Death. "
answer:
Ever since I got my badge in the Fergeson police, transferring from a small town near Seattle that you've probably never heard of, I've thought a lot about how nobody ever writes anything down around here. Literally the last piece of paper I saw was the transfer that I signed.
Now, don't get me wrong, I like paperwork as little as anybody else. But it's the things that go unwritten.
Like the instructions about who to keep an eye on and who not to. Hassling blacks is ok. Hassling Muslim-looking people is fine, good even. But white boys, especially the ones driving nice cars or wearing fine clothes, well obviously I shouldn't have to explain this. Nobody ever has to write such instructions down. The top cops, the alpha males, they instruct us by their actions. And when we step out of line, a little gentle teasing is usually all it takes to make sure we understand our instructions loud and clear.
Now, don't get me wrong, I appreciate succinctness as much as anybody else. But it's the things that go unsaid.
Like the instructions about loyalty and commitment and service. You do what the state says, you get with the program, and you obey even when it costs you. Time to send a SWAT team out to some little old black lady's home to arrest her son? Or time to rough up some journalists for sitting in a McDonald's too close to the protests? Yeah, my sergeant's an egomaniac ex-marine with a thirst for pain, but hey, better to be on the delivering end than the receiving end, right? Just get in line and do what he says, or maybe I might find myself learning lessons in ways that don't require words. Lessons that might cost me in ways that I can't afford.
Now, don't get me wrong, I appreciate leadership and charisma as much as anybody else. But when I lay awake, alone in the night, I think about the things that go unthought during the day. And I wonder what kind of a man I am becoming. Or have become.

I picked up his chain and clipped it to the bottom of my pack, turning from the place I had called home for the last 5 years. The gravel of the driveway crunched beneath my boots, a familiar sound, one that I would not hear again. I felt tears begin to well in my eyes as I passed the mailbox. No point in checking it. I thought of the mountain tops, of the long grass and the sun shining on my face, of the silence. It comforted me a little.

Good old Joe. He saw the good in me. Whatever it was that I used to be was still apparent to him, even if I couldn't see it myself. He seemed to smile up at me as he trotted along. Mans best friend. I didn't feel like much of a man. Men have dignity, pride. Here I was running from my life because it had all gone so horribly wrong. Anger filled my mind for a moment, but with nowhere to go it faded. I tightened the straps on my pack and felt for my tent and sleeping bag which were hanging at the sides. Still there. Good. " Good boy Joe" I said quietly.

The lights were half turned off as people tended to flick some off when they were leaving to indicate the day was done. I reached out my hand with the goal of picking up my travel sized thermos mug, now filled with the dregs of my favourite coffee. I froze when my hand was almost there, hearing a noise from the centre of the room.
I didn't necessarily *like* my job but it paid well. Every day me and my coworkers sat at our desks and punched data into our computers. We got up to get water from the cooler and stopped for mindless office chatter. How was your weekend? Mondays, amiright? Ha ha.
Inputting those numbers was the only way to pretend that everything was alright. That nothing had changed. But as long as we stayed quiet, we were fine. We were in control. If we didn't do our jobs then they would know something was amiss, and put a stop to it immediately.
We had it planned for months. How we would do it, how we would get away with the biggest crime in the twenty first century. We were *government employees*. We couldn't be seen to be doing anything untoward or suspected of anything.
The government thought that all its citizens were mind controlled. That the chips they planted in our brains worked without fault. To their credit, most of them did. Somehow the way our office was positioned meant that we were blocked from the rays that were emitted to command the chips. At first we worried: were we part of something bigger? But then we realised they had simply not seen us: we were overlooked.
By shutting the system down, we would be'turning off' the chips and restoring free will to human kind. The only problem with this was that people who had chips in their heads but were not attached to any system at the time of the shut down were rumoured to implode. The chips were cleverly built and were connected to the point where if a chip sensed changes in the chips surrounding it, it would implode for'safety'. Of course the government knew this but dismissed it as they intended to control the public forever and could foresee no reason to change any chips nor a reason for any chips to be unattached.
We worked around the fact that restoring free will to humanity would simultaneously result in our deaths, and had a surgeon hired to remove the chips before we shut the system down. I was due for my chip removal surgery today right after work at... *fuck*.
That noise meant that I was last in. They were supposed to wait until I had left and seen the surgeon before they shut down the system. It had started.

" Never", because in three hours time, I won't exist. I'll just be bits and pieces along with a billion tons of other vaporized material floating in the shattered mesosphere.
Before that happens though, I have my masterpiece, the culmination of my life in the production of a hopelessly overplayed three hour special done by NBC. I get shivers as I remember the view from the Comcast building. Fires and panic and...
We made it on the spot, without executive decisions, without preparation, ten hours of every single person putting in whatever they deemed worthwhile, whatever was grand enough to play for a nation that had but a week to live. As the senior producer, I melted everything down into one cohesive three hour special. I refused to watch it though, even as the panic subsided and the fires went out and everyone went home to spend their last days with loved ones.
I kept one recording for myself, to play at home. With no living relatives, it was fitting that I should ride out the end of the world on my recliner, all alone. I was content to live that out.
Before I start the recording, I can almost hear what I said before we started. *Alright everyone, let's make this count. It'll be the last, greatest thing you ever do, so put everything in it. I love you all. We're on in, three... two... one... *
Jenna and Tom were smiling as if nothing was ever going to happen. The sweat on Tom's forehead almost gave it away though. Tom began, and with his rich voice, began an introduction that made me want to cry. It was beautiful, and it reflected the hurried writers' genius. Even though I had seen it first hand, through the recording it seemed that it had it's own special, personal reflection. Jenna led off, and explained how the special would work.
I cried like a baby. The special was grand, mighty in power and emotion and I felt the pride of humanity. Vast in scope, it detailed the hard, short lives of our ancestors. We toiled countless generations, done terrible things, done great things. Life today was still hard and short for many, but many had felt the wonders of life, the specialty that we could exist in such a harsh place.
The end of the special was personal, inviting each to consider their life in the scale of the universe, how special and unique was the Earth, that we could live for as long as we did and as well as we did.
I felt content when I died.

The paper slid in front of me again. Doing my best not to hyperventilate, I picked it up. That took three tries as my whole body was trembling. Getting a pen to work was even harder, but I managed something that a dyslexic ten year old might mistake as my signature.
The man took the contract from me with a smile. " It has been marvelous working with you. Please, *please* come to me with any other transactions."

question: Nobody knew the universe was a simulation... until the year 20xx when it lagged.
answer:
**Hail Nothing Full of Nothing**
I remember the night the sky went white.
I shouldn ’ t even be telling you this story. I shouldn ’ t tell anyone. In these post-internet days, information spreads only by word of mouth, and you really can kill a story if there are no mouths to tell it.
Those of us who looked up, we who were away from our ceilings from 3:46:13 to 3:46:20 AM that day and watched the dwindling night around us suddenly catch fire, pale blue and flickering, culling backward and sickening shadows upon the sudden and impossible brightness, we know the truth.
You couldn ’ t call it day. The sun never shone so cold.
Our stunned animal brains knew the difference in seconds and snapped our unblinking animal eyes and gaping animal mouths to the horror spilt like misplaced milk across our atmosphere and knew that this was the end of all things, because it was all *gone*, all the stars and all the planets and all the ugly whirling space garbage and satellites and all the maddening darkness in between just fucking vanished into a dull persistent white light, like a broken computer monitor—and all we did was stare.
We just stared and stared and wondered with a certainty like iron in the gut, Can this be how it ends?
And then I know I did not blink.
I know I watched the void open and shut before me like a god opening its eye. First there were the stars, then five seconds of flat white nothing that threatened to swallow us all whole before one second tumbled finally over the next and night washed over us once more. Milliseconds after it, the stars flickered back into formation.
I watched it all with my eyes burning and looked around the barren street and saw a stranger with an old world phone turned up toward the sky, like he was waiting to see what it did next. (I think that phone ’ s what made him disappear a few days later, when the big-government cops came knocking on doors to see who knew what.) It was reassuring to know at once that I was not crazy, because that seemed the more likely answer. He looked at me then with the same mute shock I felt well in my throat, then toward the drawn windows of my neighbors who had not seen the sky flicker out, who could never believe that the world is really as empty and shallow and meaningless as they ’ ve secretly feared all along, even if you scream at them, even if you tell them a hundred times over, they ’ ll never believe the world is not what they think they see.
But maybe you ’ ll believe me. And maybe you ’ ll do more than watch.

question: The person I see in the mirror is not the person I see in photographs of me...
answer:
The person I see in the mirror is not the person I see in photographs of me. I know that might sound deep, like I ’ m talking about the difference in the perception of myself or something like that, but the truth is actually more unsettling than that. The truth is the girl in the mirror isn ’ t me at all. It never has been.
I call her Alice, because she ’ s trapped on the other side of the looking glass, but I don ’ t know her name for sure. I ’ ve never been able to communicate with her. I used to try. I ’ d write on the mirror in toothpaste or my Mother ’ s lipstick, but I only succeeded in getting in trouble. She never responded. At least, not in any way that I could recognize.
I used to tell my parents about her, but then they took me to therapists who didn ’ t believe me. They told my parents that I ’ d outgrow my ‘ invisible friend ’ and they ’ d just need to wait it out. But I never outgrew her. She ’ s still there, whenever I look in the mirror. She hasn ’ t aged at all, even though I ’ m an adult now. She ’ s still there, with her wide blue eyes and her long black hair, watching.
I wonder who she is sometimes, but I ’ m not sure what I should even look for. I ’ m not sure what she even is. A past life? A ghost? Was she even ever human at all? Or is there really another dimension there, behind the mirror - through the looking glass? And if that ’ s the case, am I really the only person in the world who has this problem? The only one that sees something else in there? Am I the only one that got the mix up in the reflection factory?
I worry that I ’ ll never know.
